sentences.text: This small reptile measured approximately 1 meter, or 3.3 feet, in total length.
Nearly the entire skeleton of the type species is known, allowing for a detailed reconstruction.
Fossils of R. olseni indicate it was one of the most common tetrapods in its specific faunal zone.
The genus Revueltosaurus was first described by Adrian P. Hunt in 1989.
The type species, Revueltosaurus callenderi, received its name from Hunt during that same year.
The genus name honors Revuelto Creek in Quay County, New Mexico, which served as the type locality.
This name references the Spanish word for revolution, highlighting the period's significance to terrestrial vertebrate evolution.
The specific epithet callenderi commemorates Jonathan F. Callender, who directed the New Mexico Museum of Natural History.
A second species, Revueltosaurus hunti, was named by Andrew B. Heckert in 2002 and was initially classified as a basal ornithischian.
The name hunti pays tribute to paleontologist Adrian P. Hunt for his contributions to Triassic research.
A third species, R. olseni, was originally named Pekinosaurus by Hunt and Lucas in 1994 as a basal ornithischian.
The original genus name Pekinosaurus honored Pekin, North Carolina, where the fossils were found.
The species name olseni recognizes paleontologist Paul E. Olsen.
The species R. olseni was first described in 1994 under the genus Pekinosaurus by Hunt and Lucas.
Researchers suggest that osteoderms located at the tail's end may have formed a club-like structure.
Revueltosaurus is an extinct genus belonging to the pseudosuchian archosaurs.
New skeletal discoveries support the view that this animal is a pseudosuchian rather than an ornithischian dinosaur.
Phylogenetic analysis places Revueltosaurus at the base of the clade Suchia as the sister taxon to armored aetosaurs.
The genus currently includes three species: R. callenderi, R. olseni, and R. hunti.
Recent skeletal findings of R. callenderi further suggest that Revueltosaurus was a pseudosuchian.
The Paleobi Database lists the parent group of Revueltosaurus as Aetosauria.
Revueltosaurus lived during the Late Triassic, spanning from the late Carnian to the middle Norian stages.
Fossils of this animal have been discovered in the US states of New Mexico, Arizona, and North Carolina.
The Cumnock Formation, where the type locality is found, belongs to the Chathan Group and is recognized as Late Triassic.
Revueltosaurus lived from the Carnian to the Norian stages, between 237 and 205.7 million years ago.
Revueltosaurus hunti lived during the latest Carnian stage.
Recent studies indicate that the strata containing R. olseni at the Moncure locality are likely early Norian in age.
Parker et al. (2005) suggested that R. hunti is a pseudosuchian based on a squamosal bone nearly identical to that of R. callenderi.
Irmis et al. (2007) and Nesbitt et al. (2007) synonymized Krzyzanowskisaurus with Revueltosaurus, arguing that its dental features are unique to R. hunti and not related to ornithischians or mammals.
Irmis et al. and Nesbitt et al. tentatively synonymized Pekinosaurus with Revueltosaurus, noting the lack of unique diagnostic features in the original description.

Researchers debate whether dentition alone can reliably identify early dinosaurs, noting that Revueltosaurus teeth resemble those of herbivorous ornithischians despite the animal being a pseudosuchian.
Heckert erected the genus Krzyzanowskisaurus for R. hunti in 2005, suggesting its denticulated tooth enamel represented a cingulum.

Irmis et al. and Nesbitt et al. synonymized Krzyzanowskisaurus with Revueltosaurus, arguing the tooth condition is an autapomorphy of R. hunti and not homologous to ornithischian asymmetry or mammalian cingula.
